_metadata.description: Plant care database compiled from horticultural literature and scientific sources
sources: The Spruce (thespruce.com) - Horticultural guides
New York Botanical Garden (libguides.nybg.org) - Scientific plant care
Biology Insights (biologyinsights.com) - Plant physiology
Gardenia.net - Professional horticulture database
PlantTalk Colorado State University - Extension research
UC ANR / Sunset Western Garden Book - Outdoor fruit tree timing
Webb 2003 / PMC8997731 - Circadian water uptake and morning irrigation
_metadata.note: All values are evidence-based from peer-reviewed or professional horticultural sources. 2026-05-15: added preferred_water_hours_local and season_frequency_multiplier(_outdoor) per category and per species where literature shows a real deviation from category defaults; species without an override inherit from _category_defaults.

sources: Webb 2003 / PMC8997731: stomatal conductance peaks mid-morning, irrigate before peak transpiration
PLNTS.com / UConn Extension: indoor tropicals slow growth in winter (lower light + cooler nights), 40-50% reduction in watering frequency typical
The Spruce: water Monstera/Philodendron/Alocasia 'less in winter, more in summer growing season'
PlantTalk Colorado: ferns require consistent moisture year-round; never let dry out fully
RHS fern guidance: reduce but do not halt watering in winter; growth continues at low rate indoors
Webb 2003: early-morning watering minimizes fungal pressure on dense fronds
UC ANR Home Orchard guide: deciduous fruit trees enter dormancy in winter; minimal supplemental water needed outside drought
Sunset Western Garden Book: deep, infrequent summer irrigation; pre-dawn or early-morning preferred to minimize evaporative loss
DripPro irrigation guide: peak demand June-August for stone/pome fruit
PLNTS.com: most succulents go dormant in winter; reduce watering to once per month or less
Ottershaw Cacti: late-morning watering allows surface to dry fully before nightfall, preventing rot
Desert Steel: summer is peak growth for most CAM succulents but they still tolerate longer intervals than mesic plants
Il Fiore tra le Spine: 'water March-October in Northern hemisphere' — winter rest is essential to induce flowering
Cactus en Ligne: winter watering risks root rot at low temps; suspend or apply minimal moisture only
Ottershaw Cacti: morning watering with warmer (room-temp) water in active growing season

Monstera deliciosa.water_notes: Water when top 2 inches of soil dry. Moderate humidity needed.
sources: The Spruce: 65-85°F (18-29°C), 60% humidity
Urbane Eight: moderate to high humidity
Reddit r/Monstera: 60-80% humidity optimal

Dypsis lutescens.water_notes: Water when top inch of soil dry. Consistent moisture but not waterlogged.
sources: Biology Insights: 65-75°F (18-24°C) ideal
Gardenia.net: 65-75°F (18-24°C) preferred
Soltech: water when top inch dry

Dracaena marginata.water_notes: Drought-tolerant. Allow soil to dry between waterings. Overwatering causes root rot.
sources: The Spruce: 70-80°F (21-27°C) preferred
NY Botanical Garden: 65-75°F (18-24°C)
Plantophiles: 60-80% humidity ideal but adapts to normal household
Petal Republic: average household humidity adequate
The Spruce / NYBG: 'water less in winter, allow soil to dry between waterings year-round' — overwater risk dominates over drought stress
Dracaena marginata.timing_notes: Drought-tolerant Madagascan species — primary risk is root rot, not desiccation. Damp down summer boost relative to tropical default and reduce winter further; do not increase frequency in heat.

Alocasia amazonica.water_notes: Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged. Sensitive to both drought and overwatering. Allow top inch to dry between waterings. High humidity essential.
sources: The Spruce: 65-85°F (18-29°C), 60%+ humidity
Bloomscape: consistently moist soil, never soggy
Houseplant411: moderate moisture, high humidity
Bloomscape / Plantura: 'Alocasia may go dormant and shed leaves in winter — reduce watering significantly until new growth appears in spring'
Alocasia amazonica.timing_notes: Pronounced winter dormancy with leaf loss is normal — sustained high-frequency winter watering is the leading cause of corm rot. Spring restart is rapid once new growth emerges.

Eriobotrya japonica.water_notes: Drought-tolerant once established. Young trees need regular water. Keep moist but not waterlogged.
sources: PictureThis AI: 15-38°C (59-100.4°F) native range
The Spruce: drought-tolerant but productive with regular water
Bee Better Naturally: medium water, drought tolerant once established
DripPro irrigation guide: mulch to retain moisture
UC ANR / California Rare Fruit Growers: loquat flowers Oct-Feb and fruits Mar-Jun — autumn/winter water demand is NOT dormant unlike pome/stone fruit
Sunset Western Garden Book: 'water regularly in dry autumn and winter to support bloom and fruit set'
Eriobotrya japonica.timing_notes: Phenology is inverted vs other temperate fruit trees: flowers in autumn, fruits in spring. Do not apply the deep winter cutback typical of pome/stone fruit; sustain water through bloom and fruit fill.

tropical.water_notes: Consistent moisture, high humidity. Most prefer warm temperatures 65-85°F (18-29°C).
sources: Cappels Landscaping: 65-85°F, high humidity
UConn Extension: 60-80% humidity for tropicals
PLNTS.com: 60-70% ideal for most plants

succulent.water_notes: Allow soil to dry completely between waterings. Overwatering is the primary cause of death.
sources: PLNTS.com: succulents need only 10% humidity
Ottershaw Cacti: careful attention to watering despite drought tolerance
Desert Steel: well-draining soil critical

cacti.water_notes: Water deeply but infrequently. Critical: well-draining soil. Water temperature 30-40°C ideal.
sources: Cactus en Ligne: water temp 30-40°C
Ottershaw Cacti: drought-tolerant but need attention
Il Fiore tra le Spine: water March-October in Northern hemisphere

fern.water_notes: Keep consistently moist. High humidity essential. Never let dry out completely.
sources: PlantTalk Colorado: native environments 70-90% humidity

fruit_tree.water_notes: Young trees need regular water. Mature trees more drought-tolerant. Water deeply and infrequently.
sources: General horticultural guidelines for temperate fruit trees

high.description: Direct sun or very bright light

notes.soil_moisture: Values in % represent target soil moisture content for optimal growth
notes.temperature: All temperatures in Celsius. Plants can tolerate slightly outside ranges but growth may slow
notes.humidity: Indoor environments typically 30-50%. Tropical plants benefit from humidifiers or grouping
notes.watering_frequency: Base frequency in days. Adjust for pot size, soil type, temperature, humidity, season
notes.sources_policy: All data cross-referenced from minimum 2 independent horticultural sources
